newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-WOODS CONFIDENT OF WINNING MASTERS, BUT NOT WHEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WOODS CONFIDENT OF WINNING MASTERS, BUT NOT WHEN.

text.p: Tiger Woods, displaying some of the audacity of youth and also a maturity belying his tender age, said on Tuesday he was confident he could win the Masters, but he would not predict when.

"Is it realistic? I think so. I don't know if anyone else does," the 21-year-old golfing sensation told a press conference when asked about winning the year's first major championship. "If things go my way, I might have a chance to win this tournament."

Woods, who has yet to break par in six rounds in Masters competition, was not as confident about predicting when he might win here, although many people have made him a top choice to win here this week in only his third visit -- which would also make him the youngest owner of a green jacket.
"Whether I win at my third try or my 50th try, it doesn't matter," the three-time U.S. Amateur champion said, evincing a nonchalance about the Masters that few possess.
Asked what it would mean to him to win one of the most -- if not the most -- coveted prizes in golf, Woods simply said: "Ask me if I ever win."
However, the rookie professional -- who won three of his first nine events as a pro -- left little doubt that he has every intention of winning a green jacket at least once.
"To be honest with you, I don't care what anybody else says. I just came here to win," he said.
When reminded that he failed to shoot better than 72 on Augusta's 6,925-yard, par-72 course in his first two Masters, Woods shot back: "Don't forget I was an amateur."

Woods, who recently shot a 59 at his home course in a friendly match, then said he thought it was possible for someone to shoot 59 at Augusta, where the course record of 63 has been posted only twice. In fact, no one has ever shot better than 63 in any major championship.
"You know what? Physically, yes, you can do it. Whether that's realistic or not remains to be seen in tournament play," Woods said of shooting under 60 in the Masters.
There have been only two 59s ever shot in professional tour events -- by Al Geiberger in 1977 and by Chip Beck in 1991.
"It all depends if you're hot -- and you get all the right breaks," Woods said. "When I shot my 59, I got a lot of good breaks."
But Woods also knows that it takes more than luck to score well, especially in major championships. That is why he spent last week home alone -- practicing.

"The work I did at home was definitely worthwhile," he said of his Masters preparation. "Right now I'm hitting a lot of crisp shots with my irons as well as my tee shot. I'm swinging a lot better than I was last year."
Woods failed to make the cut in last year's Masters after tying for 41st place and being low amateur the year before, when he shot five-over-par 293.
Obviously, he intends to improve on that record.
"I spent time away from everybody where I could focus 100 percent on my practice," he admitted. "And it was definitely worthwhile."
Woods also said the experience he gained in his first two Masters would help him here.
"I feel comfortable just because it's my third time here," he said. "Because you're accustomed to it, you know what to expect.
"The first time I didn't know what to expect. The slopes are steeper ... the greens are faster ... the fairways are narrower than you might think."
But Woods also acknowledged that the mental aspect of the game is crucial, especially at a major championship.
"Occasionally, as anybody, I tend to go brain dead," he said, acknowledging that that is something one cannot let happen at Augusta.
"You've got to be at a level where you feel confident about your abilities physically and, much more importantly, mentally," he said.
"This golf course is going to test every facet of your game -- especially your mind," the Stanford University dropout said as he prepared for the biggest test of his golfing life.
